items.excerpt: 记录 Isabelle/HOL 子模贪心算法形式化正式发表于 Archive of Formal Proofs，以及形式化过程中逐渐显露出的算法证明结构。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes 子模贪心算法形式化正式进入 AFP Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2026年6月30日 · 约 6 分钟 Isabelle/HOL, submodular maximization, greedy algorithms, approximation guarantees, AFP Published: Archive of Formal Proofs · 2026年5月26日。 AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 GitHub repository 2026 年 5 月 26 日我的 Isabelle/HOL 项目 Greedy Algorithms for Cardinality-Constrained Submodular Maximization 发表于 Archive of Formal Proofs（AFP）。这篇就简单记录一下我做了什么，还有实际做形式化的时候哪些地方比想象中麻烦。 这个项目研究的是有限 ground set 上带基数约束的单调非负子模最大化。在相应假设下 classical greedy 运行 k 步可以得到 1 − (1 − 1/ k ) k 的有限步近似保证，所以也有熟悉的 1 − 1/e 近似比。AFP 里还包含一个经过验证的 stateful lazy greedy 版本。它用缓存的边际增益上界来减少重复计算，但是最终选出的元素还得满足 greedy 的选择条件。 发表范围： AFP 收录了 classical greedy 的形式化构造和近似证明，还有 stateful lazy greedy 的正确性与近似保证。仓库里后来做的 StochasticGreedy 包括采样模型、近似证明和 oracle 调用次数分析，但是这些都是发表后的扩展，不属于当时的 AFP 条目。 在纸面上 classical greedy 的证明其实不长：每一步选边际增益最大的元素，用子模性得到单步增益的下界，最后解递推式就能得到近似比。但是在 Isabelle 里不能直接跳过那些一般默认成立的条件。比如 ground set 是不是有限的、当前还有没有候选元素、基数约束有没有被保持、选出来的元素是不是真的满足贪心条件，这些都得明确证明。 所以我把整个形式化分成了三个部分：具体的 greedy 构造、抽象的合法贪心步骤和最后的近似分析。先证明一个实现满足单步条件，之后就可以直接复用近似证明。以后即使换一种实现也只需要重新检查选择步骤，不用从头证明同一个近似比。 Lazy greedy 还得处理缓存状态。普通 greedy 每一步直接比较真实的边际增益，但是 lazy greedy 会保存上界，只有需要时才重新计算。我需要证明这些缓存值始终是有效上界，而且最终接受的元素确实符合 greedy 条件。这样才可以沿用 classical greedy 的近似保证。 这个定理我之前已经学过了，但是实际写进 Isabelle 后发现花时间最多的不是最后那条不等式，反倒是前面的定义和引理。哪里用到了单调性，哪里用到了子模性，哪些条件应该放在通用接口里，哪些只属于具体算法，都需要分清楚。我觉得这一部分比单纯把最终定理证明出来更有收获。 很感谢 Wenda Li 老师做这个项目时给我的指导，还有 Tobias Nipkow 老师在最后修改和 AFP 发表阶段提供的帮助。看到自己的项目正式进入 AFP 还是很开心的。 发表的时候我就想继续把一些一阶优化和组合优化的证明形式化，也希望已有的定义和引理以后能直接复用。后来仓库里的 StochasticGreedy 就是在这个基础上继续做的。 做完这个项目以后我看算法证明会更注意每一步到底用了什么假设，不只是看最后得到哪个定理。 下一篇 Schur-Complement Hessian Tracking in TTGDA 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Formalizing Submodular Greedy Is Now in the AFP Feier Lyu · Originally posted June 30, 2026 · 7 min read Isabelle/HOL, submodular maximization, greedy algorithms, approximation guarantees, AFP Published: Archive of Formal Proofs · May 26, 2026. AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 GitHub repository My Isabelle/HOL project Greedy Algorithms for Cardinality-Constrained Submodular Maximization was published in the Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP) on 26 May 2026. I wanted to write down what I did and which parts took more work than I expected. The problem is monotone, non-negative submodular maximisation over a finite ground set with a cardinality constraint. Under the theorem's assumptions, classical greedy achieves the finite-step factor 1 − (1 − 1/ k ) k after k steps, and hence the familiar 1 − 1/e guarantee. The AFP entry also includes a verified stateful lazy-greedy variant. It caches upper bounds on marginal gains to avoid repeated evaluations, but the element it eventually selects still has to satisfy the greedy condition. Publication scope: The AFP entry covers the classical greedy construction and approximation proof, plus the correctness and approximation guarantee of stateful lazy greedy. The later StochasticGreedy work in the repository covers sampling, approximation results, and oracle-call bounds. It was developed after publication and is not part of that AFP entry. On paper the classical greedy proof is quite short: choose an element with maximum marginal gain, use submodularity to bound the gain at each step, and solve the recurrence. But in Isabelle I also had to prove details that a handwritten proof often leaves implicit. Is the ground set finite? Are there any candidates left? Is the cardinality constraint preserved? Does the selected element actually meet the greedy-step condition? I split the formalisation into three parts: the concrete greedy construction, an abstract specification of a valid greedy step, and the approximation proof. Once an implementation satisfies the step condition, it can reuse the approximation proof. If I change the implementation later, I only need to check the selection step again rather than reprove the same bound. Lazy greedy adds the cached state. Ordinary greedy compares the actual marginal gains at every step, but lazy greedy stores upper bounds and updates them only when necessary. I needed to prove that the bounds remain valid and that the accepted element is a valid greedy choice. Only then can the implementation inherit the classical guarantee. I already knew the approximation theorem before starting. What took the most time in Isabelle was not the final inequality but the definitions and lemmas before it. I had to keep track of where monotonicity was used, where submodularity was needed, and which assumptions belonged to the general interface rather than one implementation. That was probably the part I learnt the most from. I'm grateful to Wenda Li for guiding the project and to Tobias Nipkow for helping with the final revisions and AFP publication. I was very happy to see it published. At the time I also wanted to formalise more proofs from first-order and combinatorial optimisation and make the existing definitions and lemmas easier to reuse. The later StochasticGreedy work in the repository builds on this development. Since doing this project I pay more attention to which assumptions each step of an algorithmic proof actually uses, not just the final theorem. items.title: 从子模优化之后继续往前：Projected Gradient Descent in Isabelle/HOL
items.excerpt: 这篇 5 月 22 日的原始笔记保留项目设计时期的叙事；该独立形式化现已以《First-Order Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization in Isabelle/HOL》正式发表于 AFP。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes 从子模优化之后继续往前：Projected Gradient Descent in Isabelle/HOL Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2026年5月22日 · 约 5 分钟 标签：Isabelle/HOL · Optimization · Formalisation · AFP 发表更新 — 2026年8月 该项目现已通过审核，并以 First-Order Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization in Isabelle/HOL 正式发表于 Archive of Formal Proofs。 查看 AFP 条目 → 时间线说明 Originally posted: 2026年5月22日。本笔记早于子模贪心条目在 2026年5月26日正式发表于 AFP，因此“继续往前”指研究项目的延续，不是“发表之后”。 Submitted: 2026年7月2日 · Published in AFP: 2026年7月2日 我选 projected gradient descent（PGD）来做形式化主要是因为这个算法本身不复杂，但是证明收敛时会同时用到光滑性、凸性和投影几何。我想把这些部分分开处理，不是只把最后的收敛定理写出来。 这个项目后来以 First-Order Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization in Isabelle/HOL 为题发表于 AFP。正式条目除了 PGD 还包含普通 gradient descent 的收敛分析、projected-gradient mapping 的残差和最优性结果，以及强凸条件下的线性收敛。这篇主要写一下我当时怎么组织这些证明。 为什么选 PGD 普通 gradient descent 的迭代是： x_{n+1} = x_n - alpha * G x_n 如果迭代点必须在可行集合 C 里就需要加上投影： x_{n+1} = P_C (x_n - alpha * G x_n) 这里 G 表示梯度， P_C 是到非空闭凸集 C 的 metric projection。迭代式很好写，但是后面每条估计到底用了什么假设就没这么简单了。 比如要用 projection 的 variational inequality 就得先处理好投影本身的性质。Smoothness 也可以用 Lipschitz gradient 或 quadratic upper bound 来表述。做下降估计的时候后者比较方便，但是其他地方可能更适合用前者。所以我先把两者之间需要的关系证明好，再拿到具体算法里用。 我是怎么拆开证明的 仓库里的 Isabelle theories 是按照证明依赖来分的，没有把所有东西直接堆进 PGD 的收敛证明。 最底层是 gradient、convex differentiability 和 smoothness 的基本结果，比如凸可微函数的一阶不等式、光滑函数的二次上界以及这些假设之间的关系。然后再把和具体算法无关的 descent、finite-sum、averaging 和 telescoping 引理单独整理出来。这样以后证明其他一阶算法时就不用重新写一遍相同的求和过程。 再往上先做没有约束的 gradient descent。由单步下降估计推出光滑凸情形下的 O(1/N) 函数值界，还包括相关的 gradient residual 结果。 PGD 这里还需要 projection geometry。先证明 metric projection 的性质和 variational inequality，之后才能处理每一步的可行性、下降估计和有限步收敛界。 然后是 projected-gradient mapping。仅仅证明函数值下降还不够，因为函数值的界和一阶最优性指标不是同一件事。我需要把 mapping 的残差与最优性条件联系起来，得到对应的 optimality certificate 和 epsilon-stationarity 复杂度界。最后再加上 strong convexity 的假设来证明距离和函数值的线性收敛。 我还挺喜欢 residual 这部分的。它回答的问题很直接：除了函数值有没有下降，我们能不能从某一步的迭代点算出一个可以检查的一阶最优性指标？当然具体能保证什么还是取决于定理里的假设。 为什么单独做 Main_Results.thy 我不希望别人为了用一个 PGD 收敛定理就得先看完整个仓库。所以这次专门整理了 Main_Results.thy 作为统一的导入入口。 里面集中放了 gradient descent 和 PGD 的收敛界、projected-gradient mapping 的最优性和残差结论，还有强凸情形下的线性收敛定理。证明本身还是放在各自的 theory 里，但是使用时可以先从 Main_Results 找需要的定理。 这样以后即使我调整内部引理或者拆分文件，只要对外的 theorem aliases 没变，其他依赖这个项目的代码一般就不需要跟着改。 和子模贪心项目有什么联系 做子模贪心项目的时候我把具体 greedy construction 和抽象的贪心步骤分开，这样 lazy greedy 就能直接复用 classical greedy 的近似证明。PGD 这边也是类似的思路，但是需要分开的变成了 convexity、smoothness、projection、descent estimates 和 convergence rates。 我主要想弄清楚哪些推导适用于一般的下降序列，哪些地方必须用到投影，哪些结论又需要额外的强凸性。把这些条件分开之后证明更容易核对，以后也更容易复用。 发表前做了什么 AFP 条目里还放了 quadratic 和 projected quadratic 的例子。提交前我主要在统一定理名称、整理 Main_Results.thy 、检查 theory 之间的依赖和 build，并完成 AFP 的文档和参考文献。那个阶段就没有继续加新算法了。 做完这个项目以后我看一阶优化算法会更在意每条收敛结论到底用了哪些条件。如果之后还要形式化别的方法，我也会先看看有哪些中间引理可以单独抽出来，不会直接照着纸面证明从头写到尾。 项目代码： github.com/lyuf09/projected-gradient-descent 上一篇 子模贪心算法形式化正式进入 AFP 下一篇 Isabelle/HOL Feier Lyu · Originally posted May 22, 2026 · 5 min read Tags: Isabelle/HOL · Optimization · Formalisation · AFP Publication update — August 2026 This project has now been accepted and published in the Archive of Formal Proofs as First-Order Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization in Isabelle/HOL . The published entry is available here. View AFP Entry → Chronology note Originally posted: May 22, 2026. This note predates the submodular-greedy entry's AFP publication on May 26, so “moving forward” refers to continuing the research program, not to work begun after publication. Submitted: July 2, 2026 · Published in AFP: July 2, 2026 I chose projected gradient descent (PGD) because the algorithm is simple, but its convergence proof needs smoothness, convexity, and projection geometry at the same time. I wanted to deal with these parts separately instead of only formalising the final convergence theorem. The project was later published in the AFP as First-Order Methods for Smooth Convex Optimization in Isabelle/HOL . Besides PGD, the entry covers ordinary gradient descent, residual and optimality results for the projected-gradient mapping, and linear convergence under strong convexity. This note is about how I organised the proofs. Why PGD Ordinary gradient descent uses the update: x_{n+1} = x_n - alpha * G x_n If the iterates must stay in a feasible set C , we add a projection: x_{n+1} = P_C (x_n - alpha * G x_n) Here G denotes the gradient and P_C is the metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set C . The update rule is easy to write down, but each estimate after it needs its own assumptions. For example, the variational inequality for projection depends on the properties of the projection and the set. Smoothness can be stated using either a Lipschitz gradient or a quadratic upper bound. The latter is convenient for descent estimates, but the former can be useful elsewhere. So I proved the connections I needed first and then used them in the algorithm proofs. How I split up the proofs I organised the Isabelle theories by their proof dependencies instead of putting everything into one PGD convergence proof. The foundations cover gradients, convex differentiability, and smoothness: first-order inequalities for convex differentiable functions, quadratic upper bounds, and the relations between assumptions. I then separated out the descent, finite-sum, averaging, and telescoping lemmas that do not depend on one particular algorithm. This means I do not have to redo the same summation steps for another first-order method. Next comes unconstrained gradient descent. The one-step descent estimates give O(1/N) function-value bounds in the smooth convex case, as well as results involving gradient residuals. PGD needs an additional part on projection geometry. I first established properties of metric projection and its variational inequality, then used them for feasibility, descent estimates, and finite-horizon convergence bounds. The projected-gradient mapping comes next. Showing that the objective decreases is not enough because a function-value bound and a first-order optimality measure are not the same thing. I related the mapping residual to optimality conditions and proved the corresponding certificates and epsilon-stationarity complexity bounds. With the additional strong convexity assumption, the development also covers linear convergence of distance and function value. I liked the residual part in particular. The question is quite concrete: apart from checking whether the objective decreases, can we calculate something at an iterate that measures first-order stationarity? Exactly what that measure guarantees still depends on the assumptions. Why I added Main_Results.thy I did not want someone to have to read the entire repository just to use one PGD convergence theorem. That is why I added Main_Results.thy as a common import point. It collects theorem aliases for gradient descent and PGD convergence bounds, projected-gradient mapping and residual results, and linear convergence under strong convexity. The proofs still live in their own theory files, but the main results are easier to find and import. If I reorganise the internal lemmas or split files later, keeping these public aliases stable should mean that other projects generally do not have to change with them. How it connects to submodular greedy In the submodular greedy project I separated the concrete greedy construction from the abstract step condition, so lazy greedy could reuse the classical approximation proof. I followed a similar approach here, but the parts are now convexity, smoothness, projection, descent estimates, and convergence rates. I wanted to know which arguments apply to general descent sequences, which really need projection, and which require strong convexity. Once those assumptions are separated, the proofs are easier to check and reuse. Before publication The AFP entry also includes quadratic and projected-quadratic examples. Before submission I focused on theorem names, Main_Results.thy , theory dependencies, builds, and the AFP document and references. I stopped adding new algorithms at that stage. After this project I pay more attention to exactly which assumptions a convergence result uses. If I formalise another method, I would first look for intermediate lemmas I can separate out rather than follow a handwritten proof line by line. items.title: Isabelle/HOL 中的 Classical Greedy、LazyGreedy 与 StochasticGreedy
items.excerpt: 原文发布于 3 月 14 日；7 月更新仅补充后续状态。子模贪心条目于 5 月 26 日正式发表于 AFP，发表后仓库继续发展 StochasticGreedy theorem line。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes 从一个定理到一套框架：我的 Isabelle 子模优化项目新进展 Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2026年3月14日 · 约 6 分钟 Updated 2026年7月 · 保留原始发布日期 2026 年 5 月 26 日发表于 AFP： 正式条目包含 classical greedy 和经过验证的 stateful lazy greedy。 发表后： 仓库继续加入 StochasticGreedy 的采样模型、近似证明和 oracle-cost bounds。这篇还保留 3 月 14 日的原始发布日期。 AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 Proof document Repository 这段时间继续做 Isabelle 的子模贪心项目后，我开始把更多精力放在不同算法怎么复用同一套证明上。最早我只想把 classical greedy 的近似保证形式化，但是后来加入了 LazyGreedy，还整理了具体实例和复杂度分析。 这篇原本写于 2026 年 3 月 14 日。上面的发表更新记录的是后来发生的事，下面仍然按当时的项目思路来写。 Classical greedy：把构造和近似证明分开 Classical greedy 是整个项目的基础。我先定义贪心序列和边际增益，再证明每一步的选择满足需要的条件，还有整个构造过程中的不变量。之后才使用单调性、子模性和 gap recurrence 推出 Nemhauser–Wolsey 的 1 - 1/e 近似保证。 我不想把这些东西全部写死在一个定理里。所以抽象假设、实际的 greedy construction 和 approximation proof 是分开的。这样以后只要证明某个新算法符合相同的单步条件，就有机会直接用后面的分析，不用重新做一次递推。 LazyGreedy：证明缓存状态没有改变选择结果 LazyGreedy 的区别是它维护了缓存的 marginal-gain upper bounds，不是每一步都重新算所有元素的真实增益。但是这样就得额外证明缓存值和真实增益之间的关系。 所以在 Isabelle 里我给它定义了显式的 algorithmic state 和相应不变量，然后证明 lazy selection 满足 classical greedy 所要求的选择条件。做到这里就可以复用原来的 approximation guarantee。对应的 oracle-cost accounting 也放进了项目里。 我觉得这里比较有意思的是证明对象不再只有集合和函数，还包括算法自己保存的状态。数学上说“用缓存减少计算”很简单，但是形式化的时候还得证明这个缓存不会让算法选错。 具体实例和可执行检查 我还加入了 toy coverage instances、executable exhaustive baselines 和一些用来核对定理边界的例子。比如 greedy 严格次优但是还满足近似界的情况，以及失去子模性之后经典保证可能失效的反例。 这些例子不代替抽象证明，但是能帮我检查定义是不是符合预期。覆盖函数的具体实例化还有 exhaustive optimum 与抽象 OPT_k 之间的联系，也能让后面的算法实验复用已有结论。 发表后继续做的 StochasticGreedy AFP 在 2026 年 5 月 26 日发表的版本包含 classical greedy 和 stateful lazy greedy。StochasticGreedy 是发表之后继续加入仓库的工作，不能算进当时的 AFP 条目。 这一部分先建立了 deterministic trace 和 uniform with-replacement sampling model，再证明采样命中率、expected one-step gain、gap recurrence 以及对应的 k -step approximation bound。 复杂度方面也加入了 trace-level 的 gain-evaluation counters、sample-size 条件和 oracle-cost theorems。这样可以在同一套 epsilon 参数条件下陈述近似比和查询次数。 不过在这篇文章所记录的阶段 executable deterministic trace 和抽象概率递推还不是一个经过统一证明的可执行随机程序。两部分各自有结果，但是不能直接把它们说成完整的 executable randomized semantics。后续的 executable refinement 是另外一阶段的工作。 这段工作对我最有用的地方 做到这里我更清楚为什么要把 greedy step、approximation proof 和具体实现分开。以后加 LazyGreedy 或 StochasticGreedy 的时候可以直接检查哪些条件已经满足，哪些还需要补新引理。 我更希望这套 Isabelle 代码以后还能继续添加其他变体，不用每加一个算法就把经典定理从头证明一遍。 上一篇 从子模优化之后继续往前：Projected Gradient Descent in Isabelle/HOL 下一篇 Metalcore Piano Lab｜从音频到谱面：一个离散化的实验（WIP） 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Classical Greedy, LazyGreedy, and StochasticGreedy in Isabelle/HOL Feier Lyu · Originally posted March 14, 2026 · 8 min read Updated July 2026 - Published May 26, 2026: the AFP entry contains classical greedy and a verified stateful lazy-greedy variant. Post-publication extension: the repository continued with StochasticGreedy sampling, approximation, and oracle-cost bounds. This update does not change the original March 14 date. AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 Proof document Repository After spending more time on the Isabelle submodular greedy project, I started focusing on how different algorithms could reuse the same proofs. I had originally planned to formalise the classical greedy approximation guarantee. I later added LazyGreedy and worked on concrete instances and complexity bounds. This note was originally posted on 14 March 2026. The publication update above records what happened later, but the main text describes the project as I was organising it at that stage. Classical greedy: separating the construction from the approximation proof Classical greedy is the starting point. I defined the greedy sequence and marginal gains, then proved the conditions for each selection step and the invariants of the construction. Only after that did I use monotonicity, submodularity, and the gap recurrence to obtain the Nemhauser–Wolsey 1 - 1/e approximation guarantee. I did not want to put all of this into one theorem. The abstract assumptions, the concrete greedy construction, and the approximation proof are separate. If another algorithm satisfies the same step condition, it may be able to reuse the analysis without proving the recurrence again. LazyGreedy: checking that cached state preserves the greedy choice LazyGreedy keeps cached upper bounds on marginal gains instead of recomputing every true gain at each iteration. But this also means the formalisation has to show that the cached values remain related to the actual gains in the right way. I defined the algorithmic state and its invariants, then proved that lazy selection satisfies the classical greedy-step condition. This allows it to reuse the approximation guarantee. The project also includes oracle-cost accounting for the lazy variant. The interesting part for me was that the proof now had to talk about the state saved by the algorithm, not just sets and functions. Saying that a cache saves evaluations is easy. Proving that it does not change the required choice takes more work. Concrete examples and executable checks I also added toy coverage instances, executable exhaustive baselines, and examples that check the boundaries of the approximation theorem. These include cases where greedy is strictly suboptimal but still satisfies the bound, and counterexamples where the classical guarantee fails without submodularity. These examples do not replace the abstract proof. They help check the definitions and make it easier to instantiate the theory with coverage objectives. The connection between executable exhaustive optima and the abstract OPT_k is useful for later experiments too. StochasticGreedy after publication The AFP entry published on 26 May 2026 covers classical greedy and the verified stateful lazy-greedy variant. StochasticGreedy was added to the repository after publication, so it is not part of the published entry. This extension first developed deterministic traces and a uniform-with-replacement sampling model, followed by sampling probabilities, an expected one-step-gain bound, a gap recurrence, and a k -step approximation result. The complexity analysis also includes trace-level gain-evaluation counters, sample-size conditions, and oracle-cost theorems. They let us state the approximation and query bounds under a common choice of epsilon parameters. At the stage recorded here, the executable deterministic traces and the abstract probabilistic recurrence were still separate. Having results on both sides was not yet a proof of full executable randomized semantics. The later executable refinement belongs to a different stage of the project. What I took from this stage Working on these variants made it much clearer to me why the greedy-step condition, approximation proof, and implementation should be separated. When adding LazyGreedy or StochasticGreedy I can check which assumptions already hold and which new lemmas are needed. I want to keep the development easy to extend so that adding another greedy variant does not mean proving the classical approximation theorem again from scratch. items.title: Metalcore Piano Lab｜从音频到谱面：一个离散化的实验（WIP）
items.excerpt: 从连续音频到可玩的谱面：起音检测、节拍网格、段落对齐与可玩性约束。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Metalcore Piano Lab｜从音频到谱面：一个离散化的实验（WIP） HazezZ · 2月7日 · 约 3 分钟 我一直很想试试能不能把一段 metalcore / prog-metal 音频直接变成可以玩的音游谱面。音频里的节奏是连续时间上的信号，但是谱面最后得是一串确定时间和轨道的 notes。所以我想看看从音频分析到谱面生成到底需要哪些步骤。 Metalcore Piano Lab 是我做的一个浏览器端原型。它可以读入本地音频或 MIDI，然后尝试生成钢琴式的多轨谱面。目前还在开发，尤其是复杂节奏的识别和谱面的可玩性都还需要调整。 现在能做什么 目前的流程是上传 mp3 / wav / m4a 或 MIDI，点击 Analyze，再用键盘玩生成的谱面。原型支持 4、6、8 keys 和不同难度。 我主要想检查从连续音频到离散谱面的这条流程能不能实际跑通，还有哪一步会把节奏结构弄错。 音频怎么变成谱面 目前大概分成下面几步： 起音检测： 先找出鼓点、拨弦和其他比较明显的起音位置。这些事件决定谱面应该在什么地方放 notes。 速度估计和节拍跟踪： 根据检测到的事件建立节拍网格，再把 note timing 对齐到网格上。否则即使起音大致正确也可能出现明显的时间漂移。 拍号估计： 把事件分成合理的节拍组。Prog-metal 里经常有不规则分组，所以不能一直默认相同的重音模式。 段落识别和模板对齐： 我很在意重复 riff 的谱面是不是一致。同一个段落重新出现的时候如果生成了完全不一样的按键模式，实际玩起来会很奇怪，所以需要尽量识别重复段落并复用对齐结果。 可玩性检查： 数学上能放下的 notes 不一定适合人打。还得考虑密度、手位、重复按键和跨度。 为什么拿 metalcore 测试 Metalcore 和 prog-metal 里强切分、密集鼓点和不规则拍号都很常见。这些输入会让 beat tracking 和 section alignment 更容易出问题，所以我觉得拿它们测试比只用节奏很规整的音乐更能看出算法的限制。 现在还有什么问题 目前是 browser-native 的轻量实现，没有做完整的 stem separation。所以如果混音很密或者好几种乐器同时在响，起音检测可能会混在一起。 复杂 polymeter、突然变速和强切分也会影响节拍和拍号估计。结果就是部分 notes 可能对不上预期的拍点，或者同一个 riff 的两次谱面不够一致。 接下来想改什么 改善变速和强切分情况下的 tempo / beat tracking。 加强 sectioning 和 template alignment，减少重复段落的差异。 重新整理 difficulty scaling，把密度、跨度和手位负担对应到不同难度。 增加对不合理连打、过大跳跃和连续手位切换的限制。 把 offset 和 latency 校准做得更细，避免谱面分析正确但判定时间不对。 我现在更关心生成出来的谱面实际好不好玩，而不只是能不能从音频里检测到足够多的事件。 项目链接 github.com/lyuf09/metalcore-piano-lab 上一篇 从一个定理到一套框架：我的 Isabelle 子模优化项目新进展 下一篇 Spring 2026｜新科研记录的开始 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Metalcore Piano Lab | From Audio to Chart: A Discretization Experiment (WIP) HazezZ · 7 February 2026 · ~3 min read I have wanted to see whether I could turn a metalcore or prog-metal track directly into a playable rhythm-game chart. The music is recorded as a continuous audio signal, but the chart needs notes at specific times and in specific lanes. I wanted to work out what needs to happen between those two things. Metalcore Piano Lab is a browser-based prototype I've been making. It takes local audio or MIDI files and tries to generate multi-lane, piano-style charts. It's still in development. Recognising complicated rhythms and making the charts comfortable to play both need more work. What it can do so far You can upload an MP3, WAV, M4A or MIDI file, click Analyze, and play the generated chart on your keyboard. It has 4-, 6- and 8-key layouts and several difficulty levels. I mainly want to check whether the whole process from audio to chart actually works, and where it starts getting the rhythm wrong. How the audio becomes a chart At the moment, there are roughly five steps: Onset detection: Find drum hits, picked notes and other noticeable attacks. These give me possible positions for notes in the chart. Tempo estimation and beat tracking: Build a beat grid from the detected events, then align the notes to it. Otherwise the timing can drift even when the detected onsets are reasonably accurate. Time-signature estimation: Group the events into beats and bars that make sense. Prog-metal often uses irregular groupings, so I can't assume the same accent pattern all the way through. Section detection and template alignment: I care quite a lot about whether repeated riffs produce similar charts. Playing the same section twice with completely different key patterns would feel strange, so the program needs to recognise repeated passages and align them. Playability checks: A chart can be generated correctly in terms of timing but still be awkward to play. I also have to consider note density, hand positions, repeated key presses and large jumps. Why use metalcore for testing? Metalcore and prog-metal often have heavy syncopation, dense drums and unusual time signatures. These are exactly the things that make beat tracking and section alignment difficult. I think testing with this music tells me more about the program's limitations than only trying tracks with very regular rhythms. What still needs work This is a lightweight implementation that runs in the browser, without full stem separation. When a mix is dense or several instruments play at once, the onset detector can confuse their attacks. Complicated polymeters, sudden tempo changes and strong syncopation can also affect the beat and time-signature estimates. Some notes end up off the intended beat, and repeated riffs sometimes produce inconsistent patterns. What I want to change next Improve tempo and beat tracking when the tempo changes or the rhythm is heavily syncopated. Improve section detection and template alignment so repeated passages produce more consistent charts. Adjust difficulty scaling using note density, hand movement and the distance between keys. Reduce unnecessary repeated presses, large jumps and awkward changes in hand position. Calibrate timing offset and latency more carefully so the hit timing is right even when the analysis is accurate. Right now I care more about whether the chart is actually fun to play than how many events the program manages to detect. items.excerpt: 从纯数学走向优化研究：一个学期的研究训练与新的问题切入口。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Spring 2026｜新科研记录的开始 Feier Lyu · 1月29日 · 约 2 分钟 2026 年春季学期我开始在康奈尔大学 ORIE 系做本科科研，导师是 Shoham Sabach 教授。 在这之前我已经做过一些 Isabelle 形式化相关的工作，也有过其他数学方向的研究训练。但是这次我想更系统地学一阶优化方法，然后尝试自己研究一个具体的问题。 上学期我主要是在 Sabach 教授的指导下读文献和学习相关理论，也上了他教的优化课程。这学期我还选了他的 Optimization for AI，内容挺有意思的 :) 我本科主要学纯数学，所以刚开始接触这些优化论文的时候还需要熟悉它们的算法定义、假设和收敛证明。Sabach 教授也有纯数学背景，转向优化研究之后一直做相关理论。这点让我觉得交流起来很顺畅，而且他愿意让我先读、先尝试，然后一起讨论哪些问题值得继续做。 这学期我们计划研究 约束优化和复合优化的一阶方法（first-order methods for constrained and composite optimization） 。目前最重要的是找到一个范围合适、可以认真推导的具体问题，而不是急着把研究方向写得很大。 对我来说这也是一次从阅读已有证明到尝试做新问题的过渡。我会把后续比较值得记录的推导和想法整理下来。 上一篇 Metalcore Piano Lab｜从音频到谱面：一个离散化的实验（WIP） 下一篇 早期项目记录：Submodular Greedy 的 Isabelle 形式化 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Spring 2026 | A New Research Direction Feier Lyu · 29 January 2026 · ~2 min read In spring 2026 I started undergraduate research in Cornell's School of Operations Research and Information Engineering (ORIE), supervised by Professor Shoham Sabach. Before this, I had worked on some Isabelle formalisation projects and had research experience in other areas of maths. This time I wanted to study first-order optimisation methods more systematically and try investigating a specific problem myself. Last semester I mainly read papers and learned the relevant theory with Professor Sabach. I also took his optimisation course. This semester I'm taking his Optimization for AI course as well, which I've been enjoying :) Most of my undergraduate courses are in pure maths, so when I first started reading optimisation papers I needed some time to get used to how they define algorithms, state their assumptions and prove convergence. Professor Sabach also has a pure-maths background and later moved into optimisation research. That has made it easy for us to talk through the maths. He lets me read and try things on my own before we discuss which questions are worth pursuing. Our plan this semester is to study first-order methods for constrained and composite optimisation . The important thing for now is to find a specific problem that's manageable but still has enough maths to work through properly. I don't want to rush into something too broad. For me, this is also a chance to move from reading other people's proofs to trying a new research problem. I'll write down the calculations and ideas that seem worth keeping as I go. items.title: 早期项目记录：Submodular Greedy 的 Isabelle 形式化
items.excerpt: 2025年12月的阶段记录；项目此后已于 AFP 2026 正式发表，当前仓库另含发表后的 StochasticGreedy 扩展。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes 早期项目记录：Submodular Greedy 的 Isabelle 形式化 Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2025年12月29日 · 约 4 分钟 Updated 2026年7月 · 保留原始发布日期 2026 年 5 月 26 日这个项目正式进入 AFP，发表范围包括 classical greedy 和 verified stateful lazy greedy。之后仓库还继续做了 StochasticGreedy 的采样、近似证明和 oracle-cost 分析。下面记录的还是 2025 年 12 月的进度，没有把发表后的结果写成当时就已经完成的工作。 AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 Repository 这篇写于 2025 年 12 月。当时我正在用 Isabelle/HOL 形式化基数约束下单调子模最大化的 greedy approximation theorem。上面的更新记录了后来的 AFP 发表情况，但是下面还是保留当时的进度。 我当时在证明什么 对于单调非负子模函数，在适当的基数约束下 classical greedy 可以得到 1 - 1/e 近似保证。这个结果一般被称为 Nemhauser–Wolsey 的经典贪心近似定理。 纸面证明里经常直接说“选边际增益最大的元素”，然后用子模性得到一个平均增益下界，最后解递推式。但是在 Isabelle 里每一步都要交代对象和条件：集合是不是有限的、贪心选择有没有候选元素、边际增益怎么定义，还有每一步到底用到了哪些单调性和子模性假设。 为什么把构造和分析分开 当时我主要把项目拆成两个 theory： Greedy_Submodular_Construct.thy ： 定义 greedy sequence、marginal gain 和构造过程里的 invariants。这里只处理算法本身，不先引入近似结论。 Greedy_Submodular_Approx.thy ： 处理平均增益下界、gap recurrence 和最后的 1 - 1/e 近似证明。 我这样拆不是为了让文件看起来整齐，而是因为构造和近似分析需要的条件不完全一样。如果以后要加 lazy greedy 或其他变体，最好能直接复用后面的证明。 写进 Isabelle 后碰到的细节 在纸面上很多推理可以一句话完成，但是写进 Isabelle 的时候就得把每一步拆开。比如集合增加一个元素以后哪些性质还成立，或者那条看起来很直接的不等式具体用了哪个假设，都要核对。 这也是为什么我开始更在意 lemma 的组织方式。如果一个小条件被藏在很长的证明里，后面要复用时还得重新找出来。 2025 年 12 月的进度 当时已经有了基本的 greedy construction、边际增益的结构引理和近似证明需要的递推框架。 还在继续处理的包括子模性假设的模块化、几个技术引理的整理，以及以后做具体实例化需要的接口。 接下来计划尝试用 locale 抽象常用条件，加入 coverage function 这样的实例，并检查可执行实验和其他 greedy 变体能不能接进来。这些是当时的计划，后续成果以上面的发表更新和仓库记录为准。 项目链接 github.com/lyuf09/isabelle-submodular-greedy 上一篇 Spring 2026｜新科研记录的开始 下一篇 我的第一个 Isabelle 形式化证明 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes Early Project Note: Formalising Submodular Greedy Feier Lyu · Originally posted 29 December 2025 · ~4 min read Updated July 2026 · original posting date retained Published in AFP on May 26, 2026: the entry covers classical greedy and a verified stateful lazy-greedy variant. Post-publication extension: the repository later added StochasticGreedy sampling, approximation proofs and oracle-cost analysis. The text below describes where the project stood in December 2025. It does not claim the later work was already complete. AFP entry DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21054718 Repository I wrote this note in December 2025, when I was formalising the greedy approximation theorem for cardinality-constrained monotone submodular maximisation in Isabelle/HOL. The update above records its later publication in AFP, but the main text keeps the progress as it was at the time. What I was trying to prove For a monotone non-negative submodular function, classical greedy has a 1 - 1/e approximation guarantee under the appropriate cardinality constraint. This is the classical Nemhauser–Wolsey greedy approximation result. On paper, you can often just write “choose the element with the largest marginal gain”, use submodularity to get an average-gain bound, then solve the recurrence. But in Isabelle I need to state the objects and assumptions for every step. Is the ground set finite? Are there any candidates left? How is marginal gain defined? Which steps need monotonicity, and which need submodularity? Why I separated the construction and analysis At that stage I divided the project into two main theory files: Greedy_Submodular_Construct.thy : Defines the greedy sequence, marginal gains and invariants of the construction. It describes the algorithm without introducing the approximation bound. Greedy_Submodular_Approx.thy : Contains the average-gain bound, gap recurrence and final 1 - 1/e approximation proof. I didn't separate them just to make the files look neat. Constructing a greedy sequence and analysing its approximation guarantee need different assumptions. If I later add lazy greedy or another variant, I'd like to reuse the approximation proof where possible. Details that needed more care in Isabelle Some arguments that take one sentence on paper have to be split into several steps in Isabelle. For example, I have to check which properties are preserved when adding an element to a set, and exactly which assumption gives an inequality that looked obvious in the handwritten proof. That's also why I started paying more attention to the way I organise lemmas. If a useful condition is buried inside a long proof, I have to find it again when I want to reuse it. Progress in December 2025 At the time I had the basic greedy construction, lemmas about marginal gains and the recurrence needed for the approximation proof. I was still working on separating out the submodularity assumptions, reorganising a few technical lemmas and making the definitions easier to use in concrete examples. My next plans were to use locales for common assumptions, add examples such as coverage functions, and see whether executable experiments or other greedy variants could fit into the project. Those were my plans at the time. The publication update and repository record show what happened later. items.excerpt: 把可验证性嵌进证明过程：从动机到 Nemhauser–Wolsey theorem。
items.content: Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes 我的第一个 Isabelle 形式化证明 Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2025年10月18日 · 约 2 分钟 Updated 2026年7月 · 保留原始发布日期 后来的子模贪心项目在 2026 年 5 月 26 日正式进入 AFP，包含 classical greedy 和 verified stateful lazy greedy。发表后仓库还加入了 StochasticGreedy 的证明。这篇保留 2025 年 10 月刚开始学习 Isabelle 时的记录，没有把后来的进展写回当时。 我最开始接触 Isabelle 的时候想试试把自己已经学过的数学证明完整写成机器可以检查的版本。当时主要在做两个方向：一些关于极限定义的基本证明，还有单调子模函数的 greedy approximation theorem。 我当时在做什么 子模优化这边我准备形式化 Nemhauser–Wolsey 定理，也就是经典的基数约束贪心近似保证。需要先定义 ground set、marginal gain、monotonicity 和 submodularity，然后把每一步的贪心选择和最后的近似分析写清楚。 这个过程中最容易被略过的其实是基本条件。例如手写证明的时候我可能直接说“选边际增益最大的元素”，但是 Isabelle 会要求先处理有限性、候选集合和最大值是否存在。 为什么用 Isabelle 主要是当时接触的老师就在用 Isabelle，所以我也跟着学了。它和我平时手写证明最大的区别是不能靠一句“显然”跳过中间步骤。 一些我原本觉得很直接的结论，真正写的时候才发现还少了前提。有时候也会发现两个定义看起来等价，但是要把它们之间的关系证明出来还需要不少工作。 我还挺喜欢这个过程的。不是因为每个小 lemma 都很难，而是它会让我更清楚自己到底证明了什么。 2025 年 10 月的进度 当时已经完成了一些关于 filter limit 和 sequential limit 的定义，以及 filter limit 蕴含 sequential limit 的证明。子模贪心那边也搭好了基本的形式化结构。 接下来还想继续处理两种极限定义的等价性，补齐贪心近似证明需要的引理，再看看能不能把这些结果应用到其他优化问题里。 这是我最早的一篇 Isabelle 学习记录。后来的子模贪心项目已经正式进入 AFP，发表范围和后续扩展在上面的更新里都有说明。 上一篇 早期项目记录：Submodular Greedy 的 Isabelle 形式化 下一篇 暂无下一篇 继续浏览 Research Statement Selected Work Technical Notes My First Isabelle Formalization Project Feier Lyu · Originally posted 18 October 2025 · ~2 min read Updated July 2026 · original posting date retained The submodular greedy project was later published in AFP on May 26, 2026. The entry covers classical greedy and a verified stateful lazy-greedy variant. Work on StochasticGreedy was added to the repository after publication. This note describes when I was just starting with Isabelle in October 2025, without treating the later results as work I had already finished. When I first started using Isabelle, I wanted to see whether I could take proofs I had already learned and write them in a form that a computer could check. At the time I was working on two things: some basic proofs about limits, and the greedy approximation theorem for monotone submodular functions. What I was doing at the time For submodular optimisation I wanted to formalise the Nemhauser–Wolsey theorem, which gives the classical greedy approximation guarantee under a cardinality constraint. I needed to define the ground set, marginal gains, monotonicity and submodularity, then make the greedy choices and the approximation proof precise. The details most easily skipped were often the basic assumptions. In a handwritten proof I might simply say “choose an element with maximum marginal gain”. But Isabelle makes me check finiteness, the candidate set and whether a maximum actually exists. Why Isabelle? Mostly because the teachers I was working with at the time used Isabelle, so I started learning it too. The biggest difference from my handwritten proofs is that I can't just say something is “obvious” and skip the steps in between. Sometimes a result that looked straightforward turned out to need an extra assumption. Sometimes two definitions seemed equivalent, but proving the relation between them took more work than I expected. I actually quite like this part. Not because every small lemma is difficult, but because it makes me check exactly what I've proved. Progress in October 2025 By then I had written some definitions for filter limits and sequential limits, and proved that a filter limit implies a sequential limit. I had also set up the basics for the submodular greedy formalisation. Next I wanted to work on the equivalence of the two limit definitions, complete the lemmas needed for the greedy approximation proof, and see whether any of this could be useful for other optimisation problems. This was one of my earliest notes about learning Isabelle. The submodular greedy project was later published in AFP, and the update above explains what the published entry covers and what was added afterwards. items.excerpt_en: A concise overview of collaborative research with Prof. Shoham Sabach and Owen Li on second-order geometry in network localization.
items.content: Selected Work Research Statement Technical Notes 网络定位中的二阶几何：研究概览 Feier Lyu · 最初发布于 2026-07-22 · 更新于 2026-08-23 · 约 4 分钟 研究参与者： Feier Lyu、Prof. Shoham Sabach、Owen Li Network Localization · Nonconvex Optimization · Negative Curvature · Structured Screening 我们现在在研究网络定位问题里可微驻点附近的二阶性质，主要想知道不同边的几何关系会怎样影响 Hessian。 这项合作研究还在进行。这里先记录问题背景、我们正在研究什么，还有目前可以公开的结论。具体判据、证明和实验还没有定稿，所以暂时不放出来，最后以正式论文为准。 最近我一直在研究下面这类网络定位问题： F ( x ) = ∑ ( i , j )∈ E (‖ x i − x j ‖−δ ij ) 2 . 我们知道图上部分边的目标距离 δ ij ，需要找到节点的位置 x i ，让实际距离尽量接近目标距离。这是一个非凸优化问题，所以算法找到 stationary point 并不代表已经找到了局部极小点。 之前已经有工作研究过非光滑 critical points，还有某些情况下从坏点逃逸的构造。我现在主要关注可微的 stationary points：除了直接看 Hessian 的特征值，我们能不能从图结构和节点的几何关系判断有没有负曲率方向？ 1. 先看单条边 最开始我想知道一条边的实际长度和目标距离之间的差值能不能决定驻点的二阶性质。这个差值确实会影响这条边在 Hessian 里的贡献，但是 只看一条边还不能判断整个 Hessian 有没有负方向 。 因为最后需要把所有边的二阶贡献加起来。一条边单独有负的曲率贡献不代表整个 Hessian 就一定有负特征值。 2. 还得把其他边算进去 移动一个节点会同时改变所有连到这个节点的测量边。所以某条边在一个扰动方向上的负贡献可能被其他边的正贡献抵消。我们需要看的是整个网络沿同一个方向的二阶变化，不能把每条边分开判断。 这也是为什么我不想只靠数值计算 Hessian 的最小特征值。这样确实可以检查一个具体算例有没有负曲率，但是我更想知道到底是哪些图结构和几何条件造成了这个结果。 3. 现在做到哪里 我们还在研究可微驻点处的二阶性质到底和图结构有什么联系，以及哪些条件能帮助我们判断负曲率。目前先不公开正在整理的具体判据，也不会把少数算例里的现象直接写成一般结论。 这个项目是我和 Prof. Shoham Sabach、Owen Li 一起做的。更具体的技术细节可以按需沟通，正式结论还是以后面的 preprint 或论文为准。 研究陈述 代表性工作 Second-Order Geometry in Network Localization: A Research Overview Feier Lyu · Originally posted 2026-07-22 · Updated 2026-08-23 · 4 min read Research participants: Feier Lyu, Prof. Shoham Sabach, and Owen Li Network Localization · Nonconvex Optimization · Negative Curvature · Structured Screening We are looking at the second-order behaviour of a network-localisation objective near differentiable stationary points. More specifically, we want to understand how the geometry of different edges affects the Hessian. This is ongoing collaborative work. I'm only describing the problem, what we're investigating, and the conclusions we can discuss publicly. Criteria, proofs, and experiments that are still being developed are not included here. The final claims will be in the paper. Recently I've been looking at network-localisation problems of the form: F ( x ) = ∑ ( i , j )∈ E (‖ x i − x j ‖−δ ij ) 2 . We know the target distances δ ij for some edges of a graph. The task is to find positions x i so that the actual distances are as close as possible to those targets. This is a nonconvex problem, so finding a stationary point does not mean we have found a local minimum. Previous work has looked at nonsmooth critical points, including escape constructions in certain cases. I'm mainly interested in differentiable stationary points. Apart from directly checking the Hessian eigenvalues, can we use the graph structure and node geometry to tell whether a negative-curvature direction exists? 1. Starting with one edge I first wanted to know whether the difference between an edge's actual length and its target distance could determine the second-order behaviour at a stationary point. It does affect that edge's contribution to the Hessian. But one edge alone is not enough to determine whether the full Hessian has a negative direction . We need to add the second-order contributions of all the edges. A negative contribution from one edge does not necessarily give the full Hessian a negative eigenvalue. 2. The other edges matter too Moving one node also changes every measured edge attached to it. So a negative contribution from one edge along a particular direction may be cancelled by positive contributions from others. We have to consider the second-order change of the whole network along the same direction, not each edge separately. This is why I don't want to rely only on numerical checks of the smallest Hessian eigenvalue. Those checks can tell us whether a particular example has negative curvature, but I also want to know which graph structures or geometric conditions explain the result. 3. Current work We're still investigating how second-order behaviour at differentiable stationary points depends on the graph, and which conditions help us detect negative curvature. I'm not publishing the criteria we're still working on or treating observations from a few examples as general conclusions. I'm working on this project with Prof. Shoham Sabach and Owen Li. Further technical details are available on request; the formal results will be in the eventual preprint or paper. Research Statement Selected Work

items.title: 从一套框架到真正会运行的随机算法：StochasticGreedy 的 executable refinement

items.excerpt_en: Connecting random bits, executable sampling, probability semantics, expected approximation guarantees, and resource accounting in one machine-checked chain.
items.content: Selected Work Research Statement Technical Notes 从一套框架到真正会运行的随机算法：StochasticGreedy 的 executable refinement Feier Lyu · 2026年10月3日 · 约 7 分钟 Isabelle/HOL · Submodular Maximization · StochasticGreedy · Randomized Algorithms · Formal Verification 我想证明实际运行的随机程序和近似分析里的概率模型对应的是同一个算法。 之前做 StochasticGreedy 的时候还有一个问题没有解决。 当时我已经有 uniform with-replacement sampling model、one-step expected-gain bound、gap recurrence、approximation guarantee 和 oracle-cost theorem。但是这些证明分析的是抽象概率模型，还没有接到真正可执行的随机程序上。 我已经证明在给定 sampling model 下每一步可以得到怎样的 expected progress，也有 deterministic trace 可以模拟采样结果。但是当时还没有证明下面这件事： 由随机比特驱动的程序产生的输出分布确实对应前面的概率模型，而且近似保证适用于这个程序。 所以最近主要就在补这个证明。 这次要把 executable sampling、概率语义和之前的近似证明接起来，不是简单地把代码和定理放在同一个仓库里。 之前的近似证明 StochasticGreedy 的算法很直接。 Classical greedy 每一轮扫描所有剩余元素，计算 marginal gain，然后选择最大的一个。StochasticGreedy 则只随机抽一个较小的 candidate pool，再在这个 sample 里面选 marginal gain 最大的元素。 如果 sample size 选得合适就能减少 full scan 需要的查询次数，而且还可以得到期望意义下的近似保证。 之前仓库里已经有对应的数学分析。 在抽象的 set-level 模型里我定义了 uniform with-replacement sampling space，证明 sample pool 命中 optimal residual elements 的概率，再利用 weighted sampling 和 expected one-step gain 的引理得到 expected gain ≥ (sampling factor / k) · current gap 形式的 progress inequality。 之后用 gap recurrence 迭代 k 步就能得到 exponential bound，再选择相应的 sample size 得到 1 - 1/e - eps 形式的 approximation guarantee。 到这里抽象概率模型的近似证明已经完成了。 但是 这里的 expectation 还属于抽象的 sampling model，不是可执行随机程序的实际输出分布。 从算法描述上看两者很接近，但是形式化时不能只凭这个直觉就把两个分布当成相同的对象。 所以接下来需要证明它们的概率语义确实相同。 先证明可执行采样器的分布 先从 sampling 开始。 我使用 Isabelle 的 executable randomized algorithms infrastructure 写了真正由 random bits 驱动的 uniform sampler，并把多个独立 draw 组合成 uniform-with-replacement sample pool。 Sampler 本身并不难写，但是还要证明它的 executable semantics 与之前的数学模型一致。 也就是说，不只是： 这个程序看起来像是在均匀抽样。 具体需要证明它的 spmf / pmf 等于之前定义的 uniform-with-replacement distribution。 完成这个证明后 random bits 生成的 sample pool 就有了与抽象模型一致的概率解释。 之前的 uniform_wr_space 只用于分析，现在还对应实际采样器的 denotational semantics。 把 abstract argmax 换成可执行的 list algorithm 接下来需要处理 argmax 。 数学证明里我可以直接写： choose an element attaining the maximum marginal gain 只要有限性和非空性成立，存在性证明就足够了。 但是这种 specification 可能依赖 Hilbert choice，没法直接生成寻找最大值元素的代码。证明最大值元素存在和真的算出它是两件事。 所以我另外实现了一个 total list-based argmax。 它顺序扫描 candidate list，维护当前最优元素，并证明： 返回值一定来自输入 list； 返回值的 score 不小于任何其他 candidate； 它对应 abstract argmax 所要求的最大 marginal gain； 实现可以直接进行 SML code generation。 然后这个 list argmax 再和 executable sampler 组合成真正的一步 stochastic greedy update。 这样 sample pool 由程序实际抽出，最大 marginal gain 元素也由 list algorithm 算出来，不再依赖抽象 choice。 从单步更新到 randomized runner 之后我定义了 recursive randomized runner。 单轮可执行算法会从当前 solution 中计算 remaining elements，以 uniform-with-replacement 的方式抽取 candidate pool，然后执行经过验证的 list-based selection procedure。 完整的 randomized runner 则使用 Isabelle executable randomized-algorithm framework 提供的 probabilistic bind structure，递归组合这些步骤。 到这里已经可以给程序 seed 并实际运行了。相同 seed 对应相同的 random bits，不同 seed 可能产生不同轨迹，而且可以 export 到 SML。 但是能运行还不代表概率分布就已经证明正确。 还需要证明整个 runner 的 probability distribution 符合抽象模型。 证明程序分布与抽象分布相同 这一部分才是我这次主要想完成的证明。 核心的 semantic result 直接识别 executable randomized step 所诱导的 distribution 与 approximation analysis 中使用的 abstract uniform-with-replacement model。与此同时，可执行开发也建立了 randomized runner 应有的 well-formedness properties，包括 almost-sure termination 与 support 中所有输出的 feasibility。 有了这个 distributional correspondence，之前的 expected-gain analysis 才可以应用到实际程序。 接着我证明，executable step 的 expected objective increment 与此前 abstract sampling analysis 中出现的 expected gain 完全一致。因此原有的 one-step theorem 不需要重新证明，可以直接 transfer 到程序： expected gain ≥ (sampling factor / k) · (f(OPT) - f(S)) 这个结果也说明之前把不同证明分开的做法确实有用。 因为 sampling、weighted one-step analysis 和 recurrence 本来就是分开的，现在新程序只需要证明自己满足相同的 semantic interface，后面的 approximation proof 就可以直接复用。 整个程序的期望近似保证 证明单步 expectation 之后还要处理整个 recursive runner 的期望。 这里我定义了 full run 的 expected objective value，并证明 recursive expectation identity：执行一轮 randomized step 后，再继续执行剩余轮数，其 expectation 可以按照对应 PMF 的 bind structure 分解。 有了这个 identity 就可以在 executable distribution 上做 recurrence induction。 最后得到 run-level theorem。 对于合适的 epsilon-driven sample size，执行 k 轮的 randomized algorithm： almost surely terminates； 所有可能输出都满足 feasibility 和 cardinality constraint； 并且同一个程序的输出 PMF 满足 (1 - 1/e - eps) · f(OPT) ≤ E[f(output)] 这里关键的不是近似比例本身。 1 - 1/e - eps 当然是我们一开始就知道想要得到的结果。 重要的是右边的 expectation 不再属于另外定义的 abstract recurrence，也不依赖假设存在某个符合条件的 stochastic process。 它对应的是 实际 executable randomized runner 的输出 distribution。 因此这个近似定理现在可以直接用于程序的输出。 具体的 weighted-coverage 实例 有了 generic runner 以后，我还做了一个 concrete weighted-coverage instance。 这里还需要处理一个实现上的问题。 数学 theorem 最自然地在 real-valued objective 上陈述，但真正 code generation 时，如果为了比较 marginal gains 把大量 real arithmetic 搬进程序，并不是我想要的实现。 所以 concrete executable layer 使用 exact natural-number weights 和整数式的 coverage score，但是 specification layer 还使用 real-valued submodular objective。 然后证明两种 score comparison 对 argmax 产生完全相同的选择。 这样程序实际运行的是 exact discrete computation，但是 approximation theorem 还可以在之前的 real-valued framework 里表述。 最后这个具体 weighted-coverage runner 同样继承： almost-sure termination； feasible outputs； 1 - 1/e - eps expected approximation guarantee； SML code generation。 这样 executable refinement 就不只适用于一个抽象函数，还可以实例化到具体的 weighted-coverage objective。 对实际程序的 oracle cost 计数 在之前的 theorem line 中，我已经有 trace-level oracle accounting。 这次把 counter 直接加进了 randomized runner。 我还开发了一个记录 score evaluations 的 instrumented executable runner。对应的 refinement theorem 证明，擦除 instrumentation 后会精确恢复原来的 randomized semantics。 在当前 baseline implementation 下，一轮对 sample pool 做 sequential argmax comparison，整个 n -round runner 的 score evaluation 有一个显式 upper bound；再按照 marginal gain 需要的 objective evaluations，可以继续得到对应的 oracle budget。 所以对于 weighted-coverage instance 现在可以在相同的定理条件下同时证明： 程序 almost surely terminates； 输出始终 feasible； 它满足 expected approximation guarantee； 实际 evaluation count 满足形式化的 budget bound。 相比单独写一个 asymptotic complexity bound，这里证明的是 instrumented execution 自己产生的 evaluation count。 接下来还想优化什么 counting development 也揭示了若干 implementation-level 的机会，可以进一步减少冗余的 oracle work。我目前正在细化 executable selection routine，同时证明这些优化保持完全相同的 randomized semantics，因此也能继承既有的 approximation guarantees。 我还在用实际执行和 benchmark 比较形式化的 cost model 和运行时间。两者不是同一个指标，还需要分开看。 这次最想记录的结果 之前这个项目已经从 classical greedy 扩展到了 LazyGreedy 和 StochasticGreedy。 但是这次还需要解决程序与概率模型之间的对应关系。 仅仅在同一个仓库里放 theorem 和 executable code 还不能说明程序满足那些定理。 我这次想证明的是下面这条关系： mathematical specification → executable implementation → probability semantics → expected progress → global approximation theorem → concrete executable instance → resource accounting 每一步之间都需要对应的 theorem。 这也是为什么需要 executable refinement，不能只生成代码。 export_code 本身并不难，写一个随机程序也不难，证明一个 abstract expectation inequality 我之前也已经做完了。 难的是证明最后导出的程序和 theorem 分析的随机算法具有相同的概率语义。 发表范围： 2026 年 AFP 正式发表的是 classical greedy 和 verified stateful lazy-greedy。这篇记录的 StochasticGreedy executable randomized semantics、run-level approximation 和 resource accounting 都是发表之后继续做的扩展。 继续浏览 研究陈述 代表性工作 技术笔记 From a Framework to a Randomized Algorithm That Actually Runs: Executable Refinement of StochasticGreedy Feier Lyu · October 3, 2026 · ~7 min read Isabelle/HOL · Submodular Maximization · StochasticGreedy · Randomized Algorithms · Formal Verification Putting the algorithm, its probability semantics, its approximation proof, and executable code into one machine-checked chain. There was one problem I had not settled in the earlier StochasticGreedy development. The theorem-level development of StochasticGreedy was already fairly complete: a uniform-with-replacement sampling model, a one-step expected-gain bound, a gap recurrence, the final approximation guarantee, and an oracle-cost theorem were all in place. But the probability analysis was still separate from an actually executable stochastic algorithm. In other words, I had proved that if each step followed the sampling model, then it made the required expected progress. I also had deterministic traces that could simulate sampled outcomes. But I had not yet proved this: The probability distribution produced by a real program driven by random bits is exactly the model used in the earlier analysis, and the final approximation guarantee belongs to that very same program. So the next step was to prove that connection. I wanted to connect the executable sampling semantics to the existing approximation proof, not just keep theorems and code in the same repository. What the earlier proof established The idea behind StochasticGreedy is simple. Classical greedy scans every remaining element in each round, computes every marginal gain, and chooses the largest. StochasticGreedy samples a much smaller candidate pool and chooses the element with maximum marginal gain only within that sample. With an appropriate sample size, it uses far fewer queries than a full scan while retaining, in expectation, an approximation guarantee close to classical greedy. The repository already contained the full mathematical analysis. In a set-level abstract model, I defined a uniform-with-replacement sampling space and proved the probability that the sampled pool hits the optimal residual elements. Weighted sampling and an expected one-step-gain interface then turned that probability into a progress inequality of the form expected gain ≥ (sampling factor / k) · current gap The familiar recurrence follows. The current solution has a gap from OPT ; every step removes a fixed fraction of that gap in expectation; after k iterations, this yields an exponential bound; instantiating the sample size then gives a 1 - 1/e - eps -style approximation guarantee. That completed the proof for the abstract sampling model. The problem was that the expectation still belonged to an abstract sampling model, not to the output distribution of an executable randomized program. The algorithms look equivalent from their descriptions, but that does not prove the output distributions agree. The next task was to prove that equality. Proving the executable sampler's distribution I started with sampling. Using Isabelle's infrastructure for executable randomized algorithms, I implemented a uniform sampler driven by actual random bits and combined independent draws into a uniform-with-replacement sample pool. The sampler was straightforward to write, but I also needed to prove that its executable semantics agrees with the earlier mathematical model. The claim is not merely: This program looks as though it samples uniformly. Instead, the corresponding spmf / pmf is formally proved equal to the previously defined uniform-with-replacement distribution. At that point, random bits, the executable sampler, and the abstract sample space are connected for the first time. This distinction matters to me. Previously, uniform_wr_space was an object of analysis. It is now also the denotational semantics of a real program. Replacing abstract argmax with a list algorithm The next problem was argmax . In a purely mathematical proof, I can write: choose an element attaining the maximum marginal gain Once finiteness and nonemptiness are established, an existence proof is enough. Such a specification often relies on Hilbert choice. That works as a mathematical specification, but it does not give code generation a way to find the maximiser. I therefore implemented a total, list-based argmax. It scans the candidate list, maintains the current best element, and comes with proofs that: the returned element belongs to the input list; its score is at least that of every other candidate; it realizes the maximum marginal gain required by the abstract argmax; and the implementation supports direct SML code generation. The list argmax is then combined with the executable sampler to form a genuine stochastic-greedy update. At this point, the program no longer depends on any abstract choice: the sample pool is actually drawn, and the maximum-marginal-gain element is actually computed. From a single step to a randomised runner The next object is a recursive randomized runner. A single executable round computes the remaining elements, samples a candidate pool uniformly with replacement, and applies the verified list-based selection procedure. The full randomized runner then composes these steps recursively using the probabilistic bind structure provided by Isabelle's executable randomized-algorithm framework. It can now be given a seed and actually run. The same seed determines the same random bits; different seeds can produce different stochastic trajectories; and the complete algorithm can be exported to SML. But a working program does not by itself establish the output distribution. To call it verified stochastic greedy, I still needed to prove that the entire output distribution of the runner is the right one. Proving the program and model distributions agree This was the main proof I wanted to complete. The central semantic result identifies the distribution induced by the executable randomized step with the abstract uniform-with-replacement model used in the approximation analysis. Along the way, the executable development establishes the expected well-formedness properties of the randomized runner, including almost-sure termination and feasibility of supported outputs. This distributional correspondence is the bridge that allows the existing expected-gain analysis to be reused for the actual executable program. I then prove that the expected objective increment of the executable step is exactly the expected gain appearing in the earlier abstract sampling analysis. This allows the abstract one-step progress bound to transfer directly to the executable program: expected gain ≥ (sampling factor / k) · (f(OPT) - f(S)) Separating sampling, one-step analysis, and recurrence turned out to be useful. Once the executable step satisfies the same semantic interface, I can reuse the approximation proof. The approximation bound for the full program After connecting the single-step expectation, the next task is to propagate expectation through the full recursive runner. I define the expected objective value of a full run and prove a recursive expectation identity: after one randomized step, the expectation of the remaining run decomposes according to the bind structure of the corresponding PMF. This identity makes it possible to carry out the recurrence induction directly over the executable distribution. The final result is a run-level theorem. For the appropriate epsilon-driven sample size, the k -round randomized algorithm: terminates almost surely; produces only feasible outputs satisfying the cardinality constraint; and has an output PMF satisfying (1 - 1/e - eps) · f(OPT) ≤ E[f(output)] The important point is not the approximation ratio itself. 1 - 1/e - eps was the target from the beginning. What has changed is the right-hand side. This expectation no longer belongs to a manually defined abstract recurrence or to a hypothetical stochastic process satisfying a one-step assumption. It is the output distribution of the executable randomized runner. The expected approximation theorem now applies to the executable runner's output. A concrete weighted-coverage instance With the generic runner in place, I also built a concrete weighted-coverage instance. There is another implementation detail here. The mathematical theorem is most naturally stated for a real-valued objective. For code generation, however, I did not want marginal-gain comparisons to carry unnecessary real arithmetic into the implementation. The concrete executable layer therefore uses exact natural-number weights and an integer coverage score, while the specification layer retains the real-valued submodular objective. I then prove that the two score comparisons cause argmax to make exactly the same choices. The program consequently performs simple exact discrete computation, while the approximation theorem remains stated in the original real-valued mathematical framework. The resulting weighted-coverage runner inherits: almost-sure termination; feasible outputs; the 1 - 1/e - eps expected approximation guarantee; and SML code generation. So the refinement can also be instantiated with a concrete weighted-coverage objective. Counting oracle work in the actual program The earlier theorem line already contained trace-level oracle accounting. This time, I moved the counter into the randomized runner itself. I also developed an instrumented version of the executable runner that records score evaluations. A refinement theorem shows that erasing the instrumentation recovers the original randomized semantics exactly. For the current baseline implementation, sequential argmax comparison over one sample pool gives an explicit upper bound on score evaluations for the full n -round runner. Accounting for the objective evaluations required by a marginal gain then yields the corresponding oracle budget. For the weighted-coverage instance, the same theorem package can now state that: the program terminates almost surely; every output is feasible; the expected approximation guarantee holds; and the actual evaluation count satisfies a formal budget bound. This proves a bound on the evaluation count produced by the instrumented program, rather than only stating an asymptotic expression next to it. What I want to improve next The counting development also revealed several implementation-level opportunities for reducing redundant oracle work. I am currently refining the executable selection routine while proving that these optimizations preserve the same randomized semantics and therefore inherit the existing approximation guarantees. This part of the project is closer to verified performance engineering than to the approximation theorem itself. I am also beginning to use concrete executions and benchmarks to study how the formally verified cost model relates to practical runtime behaviour. What I wanted to record The project already covered classical greedy, LazyGreedy, and StochasticGreedy. But the executable implementation still needed a connection to the abstract probability model. Having theorems and executable code in the same repository is not enough to show that the code satisfies those theorems. The main relationships I wanted to prove were: mathematical specification → executable implementation → probability semantics → expected progress → global approximation theorem → concrete executable instance → resource accounting Every arrow in that chain is itself a theorem. This is why the executable refinement matters to the proof. export_code is not difficult by itself. Writing a randomized program is not difficult either, and I had already proved the abstract expectation inequality. The difficult part is proving that the program eventually exported is genuinely the same randomized algorithm analyzed by the theorem. The question is whether the program I actually run is the one covered by the mathematical guarantee. I want to continue working on that connection between executable algorithms and their proofs.
